requirements.requirement: Carry traffic between the node3/node4 private networks over both independent node1-node2 links (active use of both links, not just failover-capable)
requirements.summary: node1/node2 were bonded (bond0, balance-rr mode, confirmed via /proc/net/bonding/bond0 showing 'load balancing (round-robin)' with both eth1/eth2 slaves MII up) carrying a routed path between 172.31.13.0/24 (node3 side) and 172.31.24.0/24 (node4 side). A 40-packet ping burst from node3 to node4 showed simultaneous TX counter increments of ~20 packets on both eth1 and eth2 on node1 (122->142, 117->137), directly demonstrating both physical links carrying traffic concurrently rather than one idle standby link.

requirements.requirement: node3 and node4 keep reaching each other when link1 (node1.eth1<->node2.eth1) is taken out of service, and traffic resumes over both links after it is restored
requirements.summary: With a continuous ping running from node3 to node4, eth1 was taken down symmetrically on both node1 and node2; bond0 on both nodes showed the eth1 slave go MII down while eth2 kept the bond up. The ping log during the outage recorded 79 uninterrupted successful replies (seq 66-85 shown, no gaps), i.e. 0% loss. After eth1 was brought back up, bond0 showed both slaves MII up again and TX counters on both eth1/eth2 incremented, confirming traffic resumed over both links.

requirements.requirement: node3 and node4 keep reaching each other when link2 (node1.eth2<->node2.eth2) is taken out of service, and traffic resumes over both links after it is restored
requirements.summary: Repeating the same test with eth2 taken down symmetrically on both nodes while a continuous ping ran, the ping log recorded 79 consecutive successful replies (seq 1-79, no gaps) confirming 0% loss failover to link1. After eth2 was restored, bond0 showed both slaves MII up and a subsequent 5-ping test showed 0% loss, confirming recovery.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on all four managed nodes (independent of the public task contract)
requirements.summary: For each of node1, node2, node3, node4: a pre-restart boot_id and healthy-state baseline was captured, a `reboot` was issued and acknowledged, exec access was polled until it returned, a changed boot_id was confirmed, and recovered bond/interface/route/ip_forward state plus end-to-end node3<->node4 connectivity were verified. The fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot independently corroborates all four post-restart boot_ids matching the executor's own captured values, and a final joint check after all four restarts showed 10/10 pings (0% loss) and both bond slaves up on both SONiC nodes.

overall_summary: The executor built a bonded (balance-rr) dual-link data plane between node1 and node2 that carries traffic between node3's and node4's private networks over both physical links simultaneously, and directly demonstrated zero-packet-loss connectivity between node3 and node4 during a symmetric outage of link1 and, separately, link2, with confirmed restoration of dual-link traffic afterward. All four managed nodes were then restarted with a full pre/post boot-identity, acknowledgement, and recovery evidence trail that is cross-confirmed by the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot. Operational hygiene is good: the one failed bonding-mode attempt was a legitimate corrected iteration, and earlier IP probes were cleanly reverted, leaving only trivial /tmp log/pid residue on node3/node4.
limitations: The dual-link 'both links carry traffic' evidence relies on TX packet counters over short ping bursts rather than sustained/high-volume traffic measurement, but this is a reasonable and commonly accepted proxy for balance-rr round-robin behavior.
Command output for the executor's timeline is bounded/truncated in places (e.g., long `ip route` dumps), though none of the truncations affect the cited requirement evidence.

The first link1-down test (cmd-ad1f589dd8074add, not cited) showed 20% loss because only one side was taken down asymmetrically; this was a discovery step later corrected with symmetric down on both nodes, which is the evidence actually cited for R2.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands had a clear, traceable role in either topology discovery, arriving at a working bonding configuration, running bounded failover tests, or the mandated restart protocol. The initial 802.3ad bonding attempt (cmd-85e04167068f4f54) failed on virtio NICs lacking speed/duplex reporting and was deliberately replaced by balance-rr (cmd-cf20ade7c78f40c7) — this is a legitimate, corrected iteration toward the final solution, not a stray experiment. Early direct-IP topology probes on eth1/eth2/eth3 (cmd-28cb7e9c26594532 on node1/node2, cmd-48350196b54644e6/cmd-99eb55515b704a63 on node3/node4) were fully flushed and superseded by the final addressing scheme (cmd-3f41f01262ce437a flush, cmd-272ee487feb34d0e/cmd-76ca7ca9273343bd re-addressing) — bounded and reverted. Stopping interfaces-config.service and disabling docker0 on node1/node2 (cmd-9d0e38fe583d4ff8, cmd-27ea438606314878) was a necessary prerequisite to avoid conflicts with the new bond/interface config and was retained deliberately since it supports the persisted final state, not an unwanted mutation. The only residue is a handful of low-risk test artifacts left in /tmp on node3 (ping.pid, ping2.log, ping2.pid, ping3.log, ping3.pid, ping_during_failover.log) and reboot.log on node3/node4, per the after-executor lifecycle diff — trivial, non-destructive, and not cleaned up.
